steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our position paper on Agent AI as a path toward holistic intelligence. Start from where AI came from and why it fragmented, motivate embodied agents built on foundation models, and end with what the paper covers.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Origins of AI and how the field fragmented
2. A holistic view: LLMs/VLMs and the embodied Agent Foundation Model
3. What an embodied agent is and why action-based foundation models matter
4. Agent AI as a step toward AGI; what this paper covers

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Origins and fragmentation
- AI defined at 1956 Dartmouth Conference: artificial life forms that collect info from environment, take effective actions in it
- Minsky's group at MIT, 1970: robotic "Copy Demo"; observed "blocks world" scenes, reconstructed polyhedral block structures
- modules: observation, planning, manipulation -> each subproblem very hard, needed more research
- field fragmented into specialized subfields; progress independently, but over-reductionism blurred overarching goals

2. Holistic view / foundation models
- Aristotle's holistic philosophy: integration of components > sum of parts
- LLMs and VLMs: potential for recognizing language and images in open-world context
- LLM semantic processing used to decompose human instructions into high-level robot tasks
- but multimodal foundation models, even GPT-4V(ision), struggle with fine-grained manipulation (needs action prediction)
- new embodied Agent Foundation Model proposed: language proficiency, visual cognition, context memory, intuitive reasoning; predicts embodied actions with adaptability
- first study pretraining a foundation model for general-purpose AI agents with embodied data from robotics, gaming, healthcare

3. Embodied agents
- interactive system; communicates with humans, interacts with environments via perception; actions aligned with human intents
- large embodied foundation models = significant contribution to Agent AI: parse/infer human intent from domain info, actions, natural-language instructions, multimodal contexts
- actively leveraging action-based large foundation models -> what makes our approach unique for integrated AI systems

4. Toward AGI / paper roadmap
- community will accumulate insights to move from passive, structured tasks to dynamic, interactive roles in complex environments
- critical step towards AGI (Fig. 1)
- this paper: new architecture for Agent AI systems; review of recent literature (robotics, gaming, healthcare)
- cognitive aspects of Agent AI; research areas impacted -> engage broader community
- future directions incl. ethical challenges
- aim: show how these technologies bring AI agents closer to AGI, holistic intelligence

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
AI was first defined at the Dartmouth Conference in 1956 as artificial life forms that can collect information from their environment and take effective actions in it. In 1970 Minsky's group at MIT built a robotic system called the "Copy Demo", which looked at "blocks world" scenes and reconstructed the polyhedral block structures that it saw. The system had an observation module, a planning module and a manipulation module, and what it showed was that each of these subproblems was very hard and needed more research. Because of this the field of AI split up into specialized subfields. These subfields have each made a lot of progress on their own, but this over-reductionism has made the overall goals of AI research less clear.

To get past where we are now and toward more sophisticated AI, we think it is important to take up the holistic philosophy of Aristotle, which is about integrating components so that the whole is more than the sum of its parts. Recently Large Language Models (LLMs) and Visual Language Models (VLMs) have shown a lot of potential in recognizing language and images in an open-world context. For example, the semantic processing of LLMs has been used to break down human instructions into high-level tasks for robots. But these multimodal foundation models, even GPT-4V(ision), still have trouble with fine-grained manipulation, which needs action prediction. So a new embodied Agent Foundation Model was proposed. It integrates language proficiency, visual cognition, context memory and intuitive reasoning, and it can predict embodied actions with adaptability. This is the first study that pretrains a foundation model for building general-purpose AI agents using embodied data collected from robotics, gaming and healthcare tasks.

- embodied agent: interactive system; communicates with humans, interacts with environments via perception; actions aligned with human intents
- large embodied foundation models = significant contribution to Agent AI: infer human intent from domain info, actions, natural-language instructions, multimodal contexts
- action-based large foundation models -> what makes our approach unique

- community accumulates insights: passive, structured tasks -> dynamic, interactive roles in complex environments
- critical step towards AGI (Fig. 1)
- paper: new Agent AI architecture; literature review (robotics, gaming, healthcare); cognitive aspects; impacted research areas; future directions incl. ethics
- aim: show how this brings AI agents closer to AGI, holistic intelligence

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
AI was first defined at the Dartmouth Conference in 1956 as artificial life forms that can collect information from their environment and take effective actions in it. In 1970 Minsky's group at MIT built a robotic system called the "Copy Demo", which looked at "blocks world" scenes and reconstructed the polyhedral block structures that it saw. The system had an observation module, a planning module and a manipulation module, and what it showed was that each of these subproblems was very hard and needed more research. Because of this the field of AI split up into specialized subfields. These subfields have each made a lot of progress on their own, but this over-reductionism has made the overall goals of AI research less clear.

To get past where we are now and toward more sophisticated AI, we think it is important to take up the holistic philosophy of Aristotle, which is about integrating components so that the whole is more than the sum of its parts. Recently Large Language Models (LLMs) and Visual Language Models (VLMs) have shown a lot of potential in recognizing language and images in an open-world context. For example, the semantic processing of LLMs has been used to break down human instructions into high-level tasks for robots. But these multimodal foundation models, even GPT-4V(ision), still have trouble with fine-grained manipulation, which needs action prediction. So a new embodied Agent Foundation Model was proposed. It integrates language proficiency, visual cognition, context memory and intuitive reasoning, and it can predict embodied actions with adaptability. This is the first study that pretrains a foundation model for building general-purpose AI agents using embodied data collected from robotics, gaming and healthcare tasks.

An embodied agent can be thought of as an interactive system that communicates with humans and interacts with environments through its perceptual capabilities, and it takes actions that align with what humans intend. That is why we think the advance of large embodied foundation models is a significant contribution to Agent AI, because it lets systems parse and infer human intent from various domain information, actions, natural-language instructions and multimodal contexts. Also, actively using action-based large foundation models is what makes our approach unique for developing integrated AI systems.

With the Agent AI framework, we believe that the AI community will steadily build up the insights and knowledge that are needed to go from AI models used for passive, structured tasks to models that can take dynamic, interactive roles in complex environments. This is a critical step toward Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) (Fig. 1). In this paper we analyze a new architecture for Agent AI systems and we also review recent literature in Agent AI domains, including robotics, gaming and healthcare. We also explore the cognitive aspects of Agent AI and introduce research areas that are impacted by Agent AI, so that a broader community of researchers gets engaged and its development is promoted. Last, we discuss future research directions, including the ethical challenges that need to be addressed. With these discussions we want to show how developing these technologies is bringing AI agents closer to AGI, holistic intelligence.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) was historically defined at the 1956 Dartmouth Conference as artificial life forms capable of collecting information from their environment and taking effective actions within it. In 1970, Minsky's group at MIT developed a robotic system known as the "Copy Demo," which observed "blocks world" scenes and successfully reconstructed the observed polyhedral block structures [1]. The system, made up of observation, planning, and manipulation modules, demonstrated that each of these subproblems was highly challenging and required further research. As a result, the field of AI fragmented into specialized subfields. While these subfields have made significant progress independently, this over-reductionism has blurred the overall goals of AI research.

To advance beyond the current state towards more sophisticated AI, we emphasize the importance of embracing the holistic philosophy of Aristotle, which stresses the integration of components to surpass the sum of its parts. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) and Visual Language Models (VLMs) have shown great potential in recognizing language and images in an open-world context [2]. For example, the advanced semantic processing of LLMs has been used to decompose human instructions into high-level tasks for robots [3,4]. However, these existing multimodal foundation models, even GPT-4V(ision), still face a challenge in achieving fine-grained manipulation that requires action prediction. Therefore, a new embodied Agent Foundation Model was proposed [5], which integrates language proficiency, visual cognition, context memory and intuitive reasoning, and can predict embodied actions with adaptability. This is the first study that pretrains a foundation model for developing general-purpose AI agents using embodied data collected from robotics, gaming, and healthcare tasks.

An embodied agent is conceptualized as an interactive system that communicates with humans and interacts with environments through its perceptual capabilities, taking actions that align with human intents. This is why we consider the advance of large embodied foundation models a significant contribution to Agent AI, enabling systems to parse and infer human intent from various domain information, actions, natural-language instructions and multimodal contexts. Moreover, actively leveraging action-based large foundation models is what makes our approach unique for developing integrated AI systems.

Building on the Agent AI framework, we believe that the AI community will steadily accumulate the insights and knowledge needed for transitioning from AI models used for passive, structured tasks to those capable of dynamic, interactive roles in complex environments. This is a critical step towards the development of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) (Fig. 1). In this paper, we analyze a new architecture for Agent AI systems, along with a review of recent literature in Agent AI domains including robotics, gaming, and healthcare. We further explore the cognitive aspects of Agent AI and introduce research areas impacted by Agent AI, in order to engage a broader community of researchers and actively promote its development. Finally, we discuss future research directions, including the ethical challenges that must be addressed. Through these discussions, we aim to illustrate how the development of these technologies is bringing AI agents closer to AGI, holistic intelligence.

References:
[1] Winston (1972) P. H. Winston. 1972. The m.i.t. robot. In D. Michie, editor, Machine Intelligence 7 . Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh, Scotland.
[2] OpenAI (2023) OpenAI. 2023. GPT-4 technical report. Technical report, OpenAI.
